Discover how to stop woodlice entering your home this November with simple tips to reduce dampness, seal entry points and keep unwanted pests away.


## Why Are Woodlice Entering Homes in November?


As November approaches, falling temperatures and wetter weather can encourage small pests to seek shelter indoors. Woodlice are among the creatures homeowners may notice crawling around bathrooms, kitchens, basements and other damp areas during autumn and winter.


Although finding these tiny grey creatures inside your home can be unpleasant, woodlice are generally harmless to people. They do not bite humans, and their presence does not automatically mean your property is dirty. However, seeing them regularly could indicate excess moisture or gaps around your home's exterior.


The good news is that a few straightforward changes can help reduce the chances of woodlice entering your living spaces. Controlling dampness, removing outdoor hiding places and sealing potential entry points are among the most effective steps to take before winter arrives.


## 1. Reduce Dampness to Make Your Home Less Attractive


One of the most important ways to discourage woodlice is to tackle damp conditions. These small crustaceans depend on moisture to survive and are commonly found in cool, humid environments.


Bathrooms, kitchens, utility rooms and poorly ventilated storage spaces can provide suitable conditions if moisture builds up regularly.


To make these areas less inviting, open windows when practical, use extractor fans while cooking or showering, and allow damp surfaces to dry thoroughly. Repair dripping taps and leaking pipes as soon as possible to prevent water from accumulating in hidden corners.


If a room remains humid despite regular ventilation, a dehumidifier may help reduce excess moisture.


Pay particular attention to areas beneath sinks, behind washing machines and around plumbing connections. Even a small leak can create a persistently damp environment that attracts unwanted pests.


**Quick tip:** If you regularly spot woodlice in the same area, investigate the surrounding space for condensation, leaks or damp patches rather than simply removing the insects.


## 2. Seal Gaps Around Doors, Windows and Pipes


Woodlice can enter through surprisingly small openings around a property. Cracks in walls, gaps beneath external doors and spaces surrounding pipes can provide convenient routes indoors.


Inspect the ground floor of your home, paying particular attention to window frames, door thresholds, air bricks and plumbing entry points.


Weatherstripping can help close gaps around doors and windows, while suitable sealant may be used around pipes and other openings where appropriate.


However, never block essential ventilation openings or air bricks without professional advice. These features help maintain airflow and prevent moisture problems within the property.


Check window seals and door frames for damage, particularly after periods of heavy rain or strong winds.


By closing suitable entry points, you can make it harder for woodlice and other crawling insects to move inside when outdoor conditions become colder and wetter.


## 3. Clear Leaves and Garden Debris Near Exterior Walls


Your garden can also influence the number of woodlice entering your home.


Woodlice commonly shelter beneath damp leaves, stones, plant pots, rotting timber and other organic material. When these hiding places sit close to exterior walls, the insects may find it easier to wander indoors.


During autumn, regularly remove fallen leaves and clear accumulated garden debris from around doors, windows and foundations.


Move unused pots away from walls where practical, and avoid storing damp cardboard or untreated timber directly against the house.


If you keep firewood outdoors, store it neatly on a raised rack and away from the building wherever possible.


These simple gardening habits reduce the number of suitable hiding places immediately beside your property.


You do not need to eliminate every woodlouse from your garden. They play a useful role in breaking down decaying organic matter. The aim is simply to discourage them from gathering close to indoor entry points.


## 4. Keep Bathrooms and Kitchens Dry


Woodlice are not the only pests that may become noticeable during the colder months. Silverfish also prefer humid environments and can sometimes be found in bathrooms, kitchens and storage areas.


Maintaining a clean, dry home can help discourage both.


After showering, wipe away excess water where practical and allow the bathroom to ventilate properly. Avoid leaving wet towels or damp laundry piled up for long periods.


In the kitchen, clean spills promptly, empty rubbish bins regularly and check beneath appliances for moisture or food debris.


Store dry foods in sealed containers to reduce access for pantry pests, although food is not the main attraction for woodlice.


Regular vacuuming can also remove dust and debris that provide food for certain household insects.


Remember that different pests have different habits, so identifying the insect correctly can help you choose the most appropriate prevention method.


## 5. Use Sticky Traps to Monitor Pest Activity


If woodlice or silverfish continue appearing indoors, monitoring their activity can help you understand where they are coming from.


Sticky insect traps can be placed along skirting boards, beneath sinks or behind appliances, following the manufacturer's instructions.


These traps may help capture crawling insects and reveal which areas experience the most activity. However, they will not address the underlying cause if dampness or an entry point remains.


Check traps regularly and investigate nearby cracks, leaks and concealed spaces if insects repeatedly appear in the same location.


For woodlice, reducing moisture and blocking suitable entry routes should remain the main priorities.


If the problem persists despite these measures, consider contacting a qualified pest control professional who can assess the property and recommend an appropriate treatment.


## 6. Avoid Relying on Insecticides Alone


Insecticidal sprays and powders are available for certain household pest problems, but they should not automatically be the first solution for occasional woodlice sightings.


If insects are entering because of a leak, persistent humidity or an opening around a door, chemical treatments alone may provide only temporary relief.


Start with practical prevention measures and assess whether the number of sightings decreases.


If you decide to use a pest control product, check that it is suitable for the specific insect and intended location. Read and follow all label instructions carefully, and keep treatments away from children, pets, food preparation surfaces and water sources as directed.


Never apply chemicals in ways that are not permitted by the product label.


Where there is a persistent infestation, professional advice can help establish whether treatment is necessary and identify the conditions allowing the pests to thrive.


## 7. When Should You Be Concerned About Woodlice?


Finding one or two woodlice indoors does not necessarily indicate a serious problem. An occasional insect may simply have entered through an open door, a ventilation opening or a small gap.


However, repeated sightings, especially in the same damp area, are worth investigating.


Look for signs of leaking pipes, condensation, damaged seals or moisture collecting around windows and external walls.


Woodlice generally prefer damp environments and feed mainly on decaying organic material. They are not usually considered a threat to people, and a small number indoors is unlikely to cause significant damage.


Nevertheless, persistent dampness can create other problems, including mould growth and damage to building materials. Addressing moisture promptly can therefore benefit your property beyond pest prevention.


If you notice extensive damp patches, musty smells or recurring water damage, consider seeking advice from an appropriate building professional.


## Final Thoughts


Keeping woodlice out of your home this November does not have to involve complicated treatments or expensive products.


The most practical approach is to reduce moisture, improve ventilation, seal suitable gaps and remove damp garden debris from around exterior walls.


Regularly checking bathrooms, kitchens, window frames and plumbing areas can help you identify potential problems before they become more difficult to manage.


Although woodlice are generally harmless, frequent indoor sightings may indicate that your home offers the cool, damp conditions they prefer.


By making a few simple changes before winter sets in, you can create a drier, less inviting environment for woodlice and other moisture-loving pests.

Pest problems can vary depending on the property and the type of insect involved. If you experience persistent pest activity or significant dampness, consult a qualified pest control specialist or relevant building professional. Always follow the manufacturer's instructions when using pest control products.
